chapterName: Early Rome & the Kingdom: The Foundation of an Empire (753-509 BCE)

questions.question: According to the story, Romulus's men carried off the young women of which people during a festival?
questions.explanation: Rome had too few women, so Romulus invited the Sabines to a religious festival and his men seized their young women. The Sabines were a hill people living north-east of Rome.
questions.sourceQuote: So, the story goes, Romulus invited the Sabines, a hill people living north-east of Rome, to a religious festival, and his men carried off their young women.

questions.question: Who plotted the killing of King Servius Tullius after his 44-year reign?
options: His daughter Tullia and her husband
questions.explanation: Servius was killed in a plot by his own daughter, Tullia, and her husband. That husband went on to become Tarquin the Proud, Rome's last king.
questions.sourceQuote: After 44 years he was killed in a plot by his own daughter, Tullia, and her husband, the future king Tarquin the Proud.

questions.question: What was the Cloaca Maxima, built under Tarquinius Priscus?
options: A covered market beside the Tiber
A stone wall around the seven hills
A great sewer that drained marshy ground
A temple to Jupiter on the Capitoline
questions.explanation: The Cloaca Maxima, or "Great Sewer", drained the marshy ground between Rome's hills. On the reclaimed land, Tarquinius began the Roman Forum.
questions.sourceQuote: The Cloaca Maxima, or "Great Sewer", drained the marshy ground between Rome's hills, and on the reclaimed land he began the Roman Forum.

questions.question: How do archaeologists think Rome actually came into being?
options: Through the gradual merging of hilltop villages
Founded in a single day by one leader
Built by Greek colonists from Cumae
questions.explanation: Rome grew slowly as several hilltop villages merged. The process was probably inspired by the idea of the city-state, which was then spreading from Greece.
questions.sourceQuote: It grew from the gradual merging of several hilltop villages, probably inspired by the idea of the city-state then spreading from Greece.

questions.question: Which invaders, who sacked Rome in 390 BC, were blamed for destroying many records of the early city?
questions.explanation: Ancient writers blamed the Gauls, invaders from the north, for destroying many records. As a result, almost nothing written survives from the age of the kings.
questions.sourceQuote: Ancient writers blamed the Gauls, invaders from the north who sacked Rome in 390 BC, for destroying many records.

questions.question: How did Romans remember Tarquin the Proud?
options: As a weak king controlled by the Senate
As a reformer who favoured the poor
As a pious king who loved peace
As a tyrant ruling through violence and fear
questions.explanation: Romans remembered Tarquin as a tyrant who ignored custom and the Senate. He even judged death-penalty cases without advisers.
questions.sourceQuote: But Romans remembered him as a tyrant who ruled through violence and fear, ignored custom and the Senate, and even judged death-penalty cases without advisers.

questions.question: What was the Circus Maximus, laid out by Tarquinius Priscus, built to host?
questions.explanation: The Circus Maximus was a giant stadium for chariot races. Tarquinius also founded the Roman games.
questions.sourceQuote: He also laid out the Circus Maximus, a giant stadium for chariot races, and founded the Roman games.

questions.question: According to tradition, how long did a Roman king hold the throne once chosen, after the reign of Romulus?
options: Until his eldest son came of age
questions.explanation: Rome's later kings were not born to the throne but chosen for life. When a king died, the Senate took charge until a new one was found.
questions.sourceQuote: According to tradition, they were chosen for life.

questions.question: What was imperium, the power the assembly granted to a new king?
options: The right to name his own successor
Sole control over the Vestal Virgins
The supreme power to command armies, govern and judge
The right to tax conquered towns
questions.explanation: Imperium was the supreme power to command armies, govern and judge. The king was also Rome's chief priest and controlled the calendar.
questions.sourceQuote: Then the assembly granted him imperium, the supreme power to command armies, govern and judge.

questions.question: King Numa Pompilius closed the doors of which god's temple as a sign that Rome was at peace?
questions.explanation: Numa closed the doors of the temple of Janus, a god of beginnings, to show Rome was at peace. His 43-year reign was remembered for peace and religion.
questions.sourceQuote: He closed the doors of the temple of Janus, a god of beginnings, as a sign that Rome was at peace.
